claims.text: The dynamic mechanical behavior of equiatomic Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by temperature- and strain-rate-dependent dislocation mobility.
Intrinsic lattice distortions in FeNiCrMn modulate dislocation mobility.
Homogenized, as-solidified FeNiCrMn can have a uniform microstructure with minimal extraneous defects.
Changing temperature and strain rate changes dislocation density and mobility in FeNiCrMn.
Chemically disordered FeNiCrMn has intrinsic lattice distortions.
Intrinsic lattice distortions create energy barriers that impede dislocation glide in FeNiCrMn.
Lower testing temperatures reduce the thermal activation available for dislocation motion.
Higher strain rates reduce the effective thermal activation available for overcoming barriers to dislocation motion.
Greater impedance to dislocation motion at low temperature or high strain rate produces higher yield strength.
Greater impedance to dislocation motion at low temperature or high strain rate produces higher work-hardening rates.
Higher temperatures or lower strain rates facilitate dislocation motion through increased thermal activation.
Facilitated dislocation motion at higher temperature or lower strain rate reduces strength.
Facilitated dislocation motion at higher temperature or lower strain rate enhances ductility.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate testing will produce higher dislocation densities in FeNiCrMn.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate testing will produce less dislocation pile-up in FeNiCrMn.
Room-temperature, quasi-static testing gives as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn a moderate strength-ductility balance.
The proposed mechanism is applicable when FeNiCrMn is single-phase, homogenized, lacks substantial pre-existing work hardening, and deforms predominantly by dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Deformation twinning may contribute to the response under extreme testing conditions.
